dossiers.argument_text:
This policy should be opposed because evidence suggests that it could reduce employment and weaken small businesses. During the Great Recession, employment fell among low-skilled workers in states most affected by federal minimum-wage increases.[F3C] A nationwide study also found that these increases made small businesses more likely to close and discouraged the creation of new ones.[F4A] Research on Bay Area restaurants similarly found increased closures among businesses operating with small profit margins.[F4C] A higher wage does not help workers if they lose their jobs or cannot find work.

Increasing the minimum wage could also make everyday necessities more expensive. Research shows that minimum-wage increases can raise grocery prices,[F5A] while a study of McDonald’s restaurants found that they also lead to higher menu prices.[F5B] Passing these costs on to customers could place additional financial pressure on families, including the low-income households the policy is intended to help.

[F4A] Raising the minimum wage will affect us all, not just low-wage employees and employers. Renkin, Montialoux & Siegenthaler found n their study of grocery stores that increases in the minimum wage raise retail food prices. dossiers.argument_text: The bottom line: the federal minimum wage needs to be raised. According to the National Low Income Housing Coalition, a worker putting in full-time hours making the current federal minimum wage can't even afford a one-bedroom apartment in most areas of the United States. [F1A] While many may consider a minimum wage job to be something for teenagers, I challenge you to think about the stay-at-home-mom who became a single mom over night. Maybe she was a victim of domestic violence, maybe even a widow. She hasn't worked in 10 years, and she can't find a job anywhere. She NEEDS a job to support her kids, and no one will hire her with the massive gap in her resume. She didn't even go to college. She's able to get a job working in fast food... at the current federal minimum wage. She can't even afford a decent place to live for herself and her children at this rate. Drexel University Center for Hunger-Free Communities says that at this rate, not only can she not afford housing to try and make a better life for herself and her children, but she can't adored basic necessities either. [F1B] These are jobs we need, and people who need to work them. If we don't raise the minimum wage, and someone IS able to do better, they will. Then who is serving you your dinner that you eat out after a long week of work? Who brings your fast food to the window? Makes your coffee in the morning? Cleans hospitals? The Congressional Budget Office has an analysis that projects increasing the federal minimum wage would lift hundreds of thousands of people out of poverty. [F2B] That's a huge difference. An increase, and all of a sudden that mom gets to start over. She can afford a place to live, and food for her and her babies. Raising the minimum wage is crucial to the wellbeing of our friends and neighbors, and essential to making sure our country is still the best one in the world.

dossiers.argument_text: While raising the minimum wage is often promoted as a straightforward tool to aid low-income workers, economic evidence shows that top-down wage mandates introduce significant trade-offs and unintended consequences. Rather than delivering uniform prosperity, forced wage floors put job opportunities, small business survival, and consumer purchasing power at risk.A federally imposed minimum wage increase applies a inflexible blanket solution to diverse economic conditions across the nation. Instead of forcing businesses into difficult choices between layoffs, price hikes, and closures, policymakers should focus on fostering market-driven economic growth, targeted workforce training, and flexible regional approaches that expand genuine opportunity without harming workers or local economies.

dossiers.argument_text: The Federal minimum wage is set in order to ensure that low-skill workers are still capable of gainful employment and that they are paid fairly. There are many small and local businesses that operate off of the assumption that they will be paying their staff minimum wage in order to ensure they are able to make ends meet. Unfortunately, the data suggests that increasing minimum wage can actually decrease the amount of low-skill jobs available, either because small businesses that rely on a low minimum wage can no longer afford to employ such positions, leading to job losses[F4A][F4B], or possibly due to business closures[F5A][F5B]. The idea that the minimum wage should be able to provide a "living wage" is extremely difficult to resolve, simply because the country is too large and varied in order to have a single "living wage" applied to all federal citizens[F2A].

This policy should be opposed because raising the minimum wage can create unintended consequences for low wage workers. Research finds little evidence that minimum wage increases reduce poverty in the long run[F1B], while other studies find that higher minimum wages can lead to job losses among low skilled workers[F3B]. Higher labor costs can also result in higher prices, especially for groceries[F4A] and restaurant meals[F4D], which may reduce some of the benefit workers receive from higher wages.

In addition, increasing the minimum wage does not affect every household in the same way. Many minimum wage workers live in households with multiple earners, so their financial situation depends on total household income rather than their individual wage alone[F2A]. Instead of relying on a higher minimum wage alone, policymakers should consider approaches that support low income households without creating significant risks of job losses or higher costs.

The costs of living vary significantly across the states. Some laws make sense to be federal. Minimum wage is not one of them. Each state should set its own minimum wage. That said, the minimum wage in states that currently follow the $7.25 federal standard really should be increased. Meanwhile, safety nets such as SNAP, Section 8, and Apple Health may offset some shortcomings of having a lower minimum wage. Increasing the wage might lead to some people losing their benefits and coming out worse off. Instead of a federal minimum wage increase, urge state increases and more awareness of social safety net programs.

All of these things would help to lower poverty.

Increasing minimum wage can have substantial negative effects on people and the economy, and these effects can outweigh the positive benefits. The policy should be opposed for a number of reasons:

* A minimum wage is a market intervention, which by definition artificially impacts supply or demand. By making the price of labor higher, businesses will try to substitute another cheaper resource in place of labor.

* Artificially increasing an input cost will lead to inflation as businesses seek to pass along their higher costs to consumers.
* For evidence of a negative impact on business, one can look to California, where fast food restaurant closures followed the increase in the minimum wage.

Proponents specifically focus on the primary, first-order effects of an increase in minimum wages [F1B]. Their analysis, however, fails to take into account the second-order effects of the implementation of minimum wage. For example, increasing the minimum wage would cause a substantial and permanent increase in prices across retail and food service industries[F5B][F5A]. If that wasn't enough, increasing the minimum wage would incentivize businesses to reduce the number of jobs they have to cut costs [F3A], and historically we see this occurred during the Great Recession[F3B]. Finally, this would result in an increase in business closures and a decrease in businesses opening[F4A], indirectly contributing to job losses among low-wage earners. Putting this all together, increasing the minimum wage would put significant pressure on businesses to raise prices and cut jobs, and in turn this would increase the number of people who are unemployed, thereby worsening the problem they set out to solve, as well as bringing even more people into poverty through rising costs who previously were able to get by.

The minimum wage should not be increased because higher labor costs can create risks for low-skilled workers and employers. A major review of minimum-wage research concludes that the evidence generally points to job losses for low-skilled workers after minimum-wage increases (Fact 3D). This suggests that although some workers may receive higher wages, others could lose employment opportunities.
It is also difficult to determine whether the current federal minimum wage is sufficient to cover basic living expenses because those needs vary significantly by household size, location, government benefits, and other circumstances (Fact 2A). Furthermore, many minimum-wage workers live in households with multiple earners, meaning their financial situation depends on combined household income rather than one worker's wages alone (Fact 2B).
Therefore, raising the minimum wage may help some workers but could also reduce employment opportunities without addressing the different financial circumstances of low-income households. Policymakers should consider alternatives that support low-income workers without imposing potentially harmful costs on employment.
